chunks.text: For two n-vectors a and b, the inner product is the number a^T b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + ... + a_n b_n: multiply the matching entries and add up the products. The Euclidean norm of a vector is ||a|| = sqrt(a^T a), so a vector's norm is never negative, and it is zero only for the zero vector. Two vectors are called orthogonal when their inner product is zero. As a worked example, take a = (2, -1, 2) and b = (1, 4, 1). Then a^T b = 2*1 + (-1)*4 + 2*1 = 0, so a and b are orthogonal, and ||a|| = sqrt(4 + 1 + 4) = 3.

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. An m by n matrix has m rows and n columns. Two matrices of the same size are added entry by entry. The product of an m by n matrix A and an n by p matrix B is the m by p matrix whose entry in row i and column j is the inner product of row i of A with column j of B. Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB and BA are usually different, and one of them may not even be defined.

objectives.label: Inner products, norms and orthogonality of vectors
